extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of ancient Greek moral philosophy; readers of Aristotle
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic framework for distinguishing moral states (virtue, vice, self-control, imperfect self-control, brutishness) and for characterizing knowledge/demonstration as it bears on moral action. Focuses on object-matter of passions, relation to practical wisdom, and how practical syllogisms underpin action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue as state accordant with Right Reason / Practical Wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue is a 'state' which is accordant with Right Reason and which implies possession of Right Reason (Practical Wisdom); virtues are not merely intellectual Practical Wisdom but imply its possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All who define Virtue add 'which is accordant with Right Reason.' Modify this to say the state is Virtue when it implies possession of Right Reason (Practical Wisdom). Natural Virtue vs Matured Virtue: the latter cannot be formed without Practical Wisdom. One cannot be strictly speaking good without Practical Wisdom nor practically wise without moral goodness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Natural Virtue and Matured Virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two forms of Moral virtue: Natural Virtue (a disposition present without full intellectual element) and Matured Virtue (formed only with Practical Wisdom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural Virtues without the intellectual/practical element may be harmful or incomplete; matured Virtue is the virtue 'in the highest sense' because it combines disposition with intellectual element (practical wisdom).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for demonstrative Knowledge (episteme)
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge via demonstration must be drawn from premises that are true, first (indemonstrable), incapable of syllogistic proof, better known, prior in order and causes of the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Premisses must be akin to the conclusion (principles). 'First' means indemonstrable; 'thesis' denotes propositions you cannot demonstrate and are unnecessary to learn something else from; axioms are necessary to learn something else. 'Prior' and 'better known' have senses relative to nature and relative to us.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive condition for demonstrative knowing: principles known better than conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: One who has demonstrative knowledge must know/believe principles better than the conclusion, because principles are causes of the conclusion and so are more knowable or lovable in virtue of being causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The knower must also be 'simply and absolutely infallible' with respect to contradictories of those principles (i.e., believe nothing more firmly than the contradictories that could form the contrary fallacy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of moral character types (Vice, Imperfect Self-Control, Brutishness, Self-Control, Endurance, Perfected Self-Mastery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral character dispositions are classed into Vice, Imperfect Self-Control (akrasia), Brutishness, Self-Control, Endurance, and Perfected Self-Mastery; these are distinct species, not merely degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach: (i) state phenomena, (ii) raise and discuss difficulties, (iii) present prevailing opinions and resolve difficulties. The list of common statements about these characters (I–VII) summarises folk and philosophical assumptions to be examined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Self-Control vs Imperfect Self-Control
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-Control is the disposition of a person apt to abide by his resolution; Imperfect Self-Control is the disposition of a person apt to depart from his resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common account: the man of Imperfect Self-Control does things at the instigation of passions knowing them to be wrong, while the man of Self-Control, knowing his lusts to be wrong, refuses by the influence of reason. But Aristotle interrogates whether failure may occur even when 'knowing' in a strict sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of Practical Wisdom to Self-Control
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether a man of Practical Wisdom can have Imperfect Self-Control: some assert impossibility (Socratic view), others allow Practical Wisdom and Imperfect Self-Control to co-exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle argues the mere possession of Practical Wisdom does not guarantee acting on it in every state; the difference can arise from having knowledge but not exercising it, or from different senses of 'knowing' (universal vs particular premises).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects (object-matter) of Self-Control and Imperfect Self-Control
rubrics_metrics.description: The object-matter of Self-Control and Imperfect Self-Control is primarily bodily pleasures and pains (those of Touch and Taste); other goods (honour, wealth, victory) are choice-worthy but, when excessive, are ascribed differently (with qualification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bodily things related to food and grosser appetites are 'necessary' pleasures and the central objects for the full species of Self-Control/Imperfect Self-Control/Perfected Self-Mastery. Excess in honour, gain, anger, etc., is described as Imperfect Self-Control only with the addition of the particular object (e.g., 'Imperfect Self-Control in respect of anger').

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope restriction: use of the term 'Imperfect Self-Control' limited to bodily pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle restricts the unqualified application of 'Imperfect Self-Control' to cases whose object-matter is bodily enjoyments; other excesses are analogous but named with qualification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because some enjoyments (honour, gain) are choice-worthy in themselves, excesses in these are blameworthy but not labelled 'Imperfect Self-Control' simply — they are 'Imperfect Self-Control with respect to X.' The terms 'soft' and similar apply to bodily enjoyments, not to these other cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account of akrasia (acting against one's knowledge): two-sense model of 'knowing'
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'knowing' has multiple senses: one may 'have' knowledge without exercising it, or have universal but not the particular premises required for action; under passion one may 'say' moral maxims without truly exercising knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical action depends on a practical syllogism with a universal and a particular premiss (the minor is sense-cognisable). Under passion the minor premiss may be absent or only present as mere saying (like a drunk repeating verses), so one can fail in Self-Control 'with knowledge' in some senses but not others. Physiological states (sleep, drunkenness, passion) explain temporary failure to exercise knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical syllogism structure as explanatory criterion for action
rubrics_metrics.description: All action can be analysed into a syllogism: a universal maxim and a particular premiss (given by Sense), whose conclusion issues in action; failure can result from using the universal but not the particular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: universal 'All that is sweet should be tasted' + 'This is sweet' -> conclusion. When competing universals or desires exist, desire can move the organs and override the practical conclusion, producing akratic action. The minor premiss's epistemic status (opinion/sense) is decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between brutish/morbid inclinations and human vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclinations produced by nature, disease, or custom that deviate (cannibalism, eating earth, etc.) are 'Brutish' or 'Morbid' and not Vice in the proper sense; mastering or being mastered by them is only metaphorically called (im)perfect self-control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inclinations are non-human in origin, they do not count as Vice simply; the presence of such inclinations is foreign to Vice. A man may have such inclinations without yielding to them (restraint), or both have and yield to them. These are treated as a different species of badness, not as the ordinary moral vices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative disgrace: Imperfect Self-Control over Lusts worse than over Anger
rubrics_metrics.description: Imperfect Self-Control arising from Lust is more disgraceful than that arising from Anger because Anger 'listens to Reason but mishears it' whereas Lust does not follow Reason and is insidious and deceptive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anger acts with pain and openness, whereas insolence acts with pleasure and deceit (examples and poetic citations). Anger is more excusable to the degree it is natural/common; lust-based failures are more unjust and disgraceful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfected Self-Mastery as union of Self-Control and Endurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfected Self-Mastery unites the qualities of Self-Control and Endurance; some say anyone who unites these is a man of Perfect Self-Mastery (though opinions vary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perfected Self-Mastery belongs to human moral excellence and contrasts with utter loss of Self-Control and brutish states; those with perfected mastery act upon moral choice rather than being driven by passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral blameworthiness tied to excess relative to Right Reason rather than object's nature
rubrics_metrics.description: People are blamed not merely for desiring or being affected by honourable or indifferent things, but for exceeding proper limits in these feelings—i.e., wrongness lies in excess relative to Right Reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even for objects that are naturally choice-worthy (honour, children, parents), excess (e.g., Niobe fighting gods) is blameworthy. Thus moral assessment depends on conformity to Right Reason and proportion, not mere appetite for good things.
